final_proof:
Let \(F:\mathcal P(S_1)\to\mathcal P(S_2)\) denote the direct-image map induced by \(f\), so that \(F(A)=f[A]\). The assertion that \(F|_{\tau _1}\) is a surjection from \(\tau _1\) onto \(\tau _2\) says precisely that
\[
\tau _2=\{f[U]:U\in\tau _1\}. \tag{*}
\]

We first prove that \(\tau _2\) is a topology on \(S_2\). Since \(\varnothing,S_1\in\tau _1\), equation (*) gives
\[
\varnothing=f[\varnothing]\in\tau _2,
\qquad
S_2=f[S_1]\in\tau _2,
\]
where the second equality uses the surjectivity of \(f\).

Let \(\{V_i\}_{i\in I}\) be any family of members of \(\tau _2\). For each \(i\in I\), by (*) choose \(U_i\in\tau _1\) such that \(V_i=f[U_i]\). Images commute with arbitrary unions, and \(\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau _1\); hence
\[
\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i
=\bigcup_{i\in I}f[U_i]
=f\!\left[\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\right]
\in\tau _2.
\]
The empty-family case is also covered by \(\varnothing\in\tau _2\).

Now let \(V_1,\ldots,V_n\in\tau _2\). Choose \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\in\tau _1\) with \(V_k=f[U_k]\). Because \(f\) is injective, direct images commute with finite intersections:
\[
\bigcap_{k=1}^n f[U_k]
=f\!\left[\bigcap_{k=1}^n U_k\right].
\]
Indeed, the inclusion from right to left is automatic. Conversely, if \(y\) belongs to every \(f[U_k]\), write \(y=f(x_k)\) with \(x_k\in U_k\). Injectivity forces all the \(x_k\)'s to be equal, so their common value belongs to every \(U_k\). Since \(\bigcap_{k=1}^nU_k\in\tau _1\), equation (*) shows that \(\bigcap_{k=1}^nV_k\in\tau _2\). The case \(n=0\) is \(S_2\in\tau _2\). Thus \(\tau _2\) satisfies all the topology axioms.

It remains to prove homeomorphism. The map \(f:S_1\to S_2\) is bijective by hypothesis. If \(V\in\tau _2\), then by (*) there is a \(U\in\tau _1\) such that \(V=f[U]\). Since \(f\) is injective,
\[
f^{-1}[V]=f^{-1}[f[U]]=U,
\]
which is open in \(S_1\). Therefore \(f:(S_1,\tau _1)\to(S_2,\tau _2)\) is continuous.

Moreover, for every \(U\in\tau _1\), equation (*) gives \(f[U]\in\tau _2\). If \(g=f^{-1}:S_2\to S_1\), then
\[
g^{-1}[U]=f[U]\in\tau _2,
\]
so \(g\) is continuous. Hence \(f\) is a homeomorphism, and \((S_2,\tau _2)\) is a topological space homeomorphic to \(T_1\).
